title: Singing scripture
hook: the Guru Granth Sahib is sung in set musical modes

segments.voice: Yesterday, nitnem: the Sikh daily round of set prayers, opening with Japji. Your line was the daily prayers. Did you read your passage at the start of the day and again before sleep? Day one thousand four hundred one.

Turn past the opening prayers of the Guru Granth Sahib, and look at the heading over the next hymn. In a novel, a heading gives you a chapter, or a topic. This one gives you a tune. Sri Raag, it says. Then it tells you which Guru is speaking. Then the words. Before the meaning, the music. Page after page, section after section, the headings change: Raag Gauri, Raag Asa, Raag Sorath. The scripture is laid out like a songbook, because that's how it's meant to be heard. Five days ago, kirtan meant a room singing names back and forth. Today, the same word, and a different thing: kirtan as scripture, sung.
screen: `A HEADING THAT GIVES A TUNE.` → `BEFORE THE MEANING, THE MUSIC.` → `LAID OUT LIKE A SONGBOOK.`

segments.voice: In Sikh life, kirtan is the singing of gurbani, the Guru's word: the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib, sung in the musical modes, the ragas, that the scripture itself names. A raga is more than a scale. In Indian music, tradition ties each raga to a mood, and often to a time of day or a season. So when the heading says which raga, it's saying how the words should feel when they reach you. Each section also names its Guru in a heading of its own. Tradition tells that Guru Nanak traveled with a Muslim musician, Bhai Mardana, who played the rebab, a stringed instrument, while the Guru sang. From the beginning, in the Sikh telling, the word came with music. In a gurdwara today, singers called ragis sit before the Guru Granth Sahib, often with harmonium and tabla, and sing its hymns. The singers don't bring new words. The words are the scripture. What changes is the singing. And the scripture speaks about this itself. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, a line says, in paraphrase, that in this dark age, kirtan is foremost. In Sikh teaching, the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru. So to sing it is not to perform about the Guru. It's to let the Guru's own words be heard the way the pages ask. Notice what music does to a text. A sentence read once is gone. A sentence sung, with a melody, comes back on its own, in the shower, in traffic, at night. Sung scripture doesn't stay on the page. It goes home with you.
screen: `THE GURU'S WORD, IN RAGA.` · `A RAGA CARRIES A MOOD.` · `MARDANA'S REBAB, NANAK'S VOICE.` · `NO NEW WORDS: THE WORDS ARE SCRIPTURE.` · then, large: `IT GOES HOME WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to listen to Sikh kirtan. After the bell, find a recording of kirtan from a gurdwara and listen to one hymn all the way through, even if you don't know the language. For now, settle, and breathe. Listen to the sounds around you as if they were music: the hum of a fridge, a car, your own breath. Then bring to mind one line, from any source, that you know because it was sung. Notice how it arrives, tune first, then words. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan. In Sikh life, the singing of the Guru Granth Sahib's own hymns in the ragas its pages name. Scripture, heard as music. Today's word.
Your line: sung scripture. Today, when a melody gets stuck in your head, ask what words came with it, and whether they're words you want to carry. Day one thousand four hundred one.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragis sing hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib in the ragas named in its headings, often with harmonium and tabla, while the congregation sits and listens or sings along.

notes: Ang 1075 line ('kaljug meh kirtan pardhana') paraphrased as 'in this dark age, kirtan is foremost'; confirm Ang number and attribution to Guru Arjan.
Sri Raag as the first raga section after the opening prayers (Ang 14); the raga names Gauri, Asa and Sorath given as examples, not in order. Confirm.
'Each section also names its Guru' refers to the Mahalla headings; confirm phrasing.
Ragas' association with moods, times of day and seasons attributed to 'tradition'. No count of ragas given under the claims rule.
Bhai Mardana and the rebab attributed to tradition (Janamsakhis).
Same index word (kirtan) as day 1396; this script takes the Sikh angle of scripture sung in raga, not call and response.
